replying_to: Replying to MECATS: Mixture-of-Experts for Probabilistic Forecasts of Aggregated Time Series
display_title: Official Review of Paper383 by Reviewer tXgU

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper deals with hierarchical forecasting using a mixture of heterogeneous experts. To do so, the proposed method learns hierarchical relationships during the training stage to produce point forecasts. Multiple quantile estimators are used to producing distribution-free and nearly coherent probabilistic forecasts. The authors also discuss an extension for situations where change points happen in the future. A comprehensive evaluation is conducted on both point and probabilistic forecasts which show increased accuracy compared to baselines.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- The combination of multiple forecasts for each series is a challenging problem in hierarchical forecasting (especially if the resulting forecasts are coherent).
- Another contribution is the extension to the probabilistic setting with quantile forecasts.

Weaknesses:
- This paper tries to do too much. I think it is better to do less, and better motivate and explain each component of your method. In particular, Section 3.2 is hard to read. It introduces multiple new concepts with few explanations.

- There are inconsistencies in your statements. First, you say "However, this approach does not perform very well in our implementation when combined with mixture-of-experts.". But later, you say "In addition, we intended to compare with Rangapuram and Taieb but their state-of-the-art implementaitons are not available.".

- Similarities and differences with existing methods are missing. In fact, your method can be seen as a generalization of the method proposed by Taieb (ERM method).  Under a gaussianity assumption, MLE reduces to Least-squares. Expression (2) is a (regularized) ERM objective. The main difference is that you are considering a dynamic and nonlinear combination of the forecasts and you allow coherency errors. In other words, if MECATS uses static linear combination (no hidden layers) and lambda_K goes to infinity, it is equivalent (or closely related) to ERM. This also suggests that you can easily compare with the ERM objective. This should be discussed in the paper. 


Other comments:
- Section 3, you say: "Ideally, the forecasts should satisfy ... ", but this is not a constraint. In other words, probabilistic forecast coherency is ill-defined in your paper.
- "Note that other reconciliation methods like MinT, requires forecasting model at every vertex to be unbiased.". Reconciliation methods do not require unbiased forecasts. Forecasts are often biased in practice and these methods still work. However, the theoretical properties are valid only under unbiased forecasts. Since you do not give any theoretical guarantee for your method, you cannot give that as a disadvantage of reconciliation methods. Please update the text accordingly.
- How did you compute CRPS? Please add a link to the appendix.
- L_v_i in (2) is not explicitly defined.
- Furthermore, you say: "Note that it is straightforward to extend linear aggregations to the non-linear case". Are you talking about problem definition or forecasting or both?
- "A model set with both high-variance and low-variance models". I am not sure this sentence if useful.
- "it is unreasonable to simply combine their conﬁdence intervals.". What do you mean by confidence intervals? Are you not trying to generate forecasts? This sentence needs clarification.
- The expression after expression (6) uses an equal sign. Should it be an approx. sign?
- Section 3.2 is poorly written. The DCT algorithm is not introduced. Please add a reference. Also, later you talk about "type-II DCT transformations" without introducing it.
- Figure 5, what is quantile coherency?
- "Building this connection to the combined point forecast regularizes each quantile estimation to be more coherent.". Why is that the case? Did you prove it theoretically or experimentally?
- "to eliminate the coherent loss". What does that mean? To make it equal to zero?
- Clearly define an "uncertainty wrapper".
- What do you report after the "+/-" in the Tables? (exact formula)

- Proposition 1: what is "coherent error"? Why are the weights between 0 and 1?
- What do you mean by "ideal value"?
- Table 4-20: why all CRPS values are in bold font?
content.summary_of_the_review: A major weakness of this paper is that it introduces too many concepts and goes in too many directions. There is a lack of focus. Clear and strong justifications for each component of your method are missing. As a result, it is hard to pinpoint the true contribution of the paper. Furthermore, when looking at the results, it is not clear that this complexity is needed given the small improvement compared to the (much simpler) existing methods. Finally, the paper is not easy to read. Writing should be improved. In its current form, I do not think the paper is ready for publication.

content.title: Response to Reviewer tXgU
content.comment:
We thank you for your comments and helpful suggestions. We agree that some parts of section 3.2 should not appear in the main text as they are too detailed. We will update that section with more conceptual explanations. The rest of your concerns are addressed below:

**Major Comments**

1. [Inconsistency of statements] There is no inconsistency, we did compare with Ben Taieb & Koo, 2019, but did not compare with Taieb et al, 2017.

2. [Generalization of ERM] This is a very interesting observation, thank you for spotting this! We did implement ERM but not from this perspective. We will add discussion and results to the main text as you suggested.

3. [Probabilistic forecast coherency] Probabilistic forecast coherency refers to the coherency of each quantile, which is defined the same as the coherency of the mean forecast. For point forecast, we incorporate the coherent loss (as also defined in appendix F.3 evaluation metrics) in Equation 2, which is a constraint, and then use the coherent point forecast to regularize quantiles using Equation 9.

4. [Unbiased assumptions] We have claimed that MECATS only requires the true value lie in the convex hull formed by forecasts from each expert. This is a weaker assumption than unbiasedness and is a more general condition. Assume we have $k$ realizations from a single model, each realization is denoted as $\hat{x}_i$; we also have forecasts from $k$ experts, each forecast is denoted as $\hat{x}^\{i\}$, and ground truth $x$ where these are all scalars. The unbiased assumption requires $E[\hat{x}_i] = x \rightarrow x = \sum_\{i=1\}^k p(\hat{x}_i) \cdot \hat{x}_i$, 
while the convex hull assumption only requires $x \in \\{\sum_\{i=1\}^k \omega_i \hat{x}^\{i\} | \sum_\{i=1\}^k \omega_i = 1, \omega_i \in [0, 1]\\}$. Obviously, the convex hull assumption is weaker and is more general as the unbiasedness is a special case. Now go back to the comparison with MinT in your comments: theoretical properties of MinT are valid only under unbiased forecasts, but it still works in practice; MECATS is valid under a weaker assumption, so it works better in practice. Please refer to appendix A for our justification of proposition 1.

5. [CRPS] It was introduced in Appendix F.3.


**Other Questions**

Q: "it is unreasonable to simply combine their conﬁdence intervals.". What do you mean by confidence intervals? Are you not trying to generate forecasts? 

A: Confidence intervals should be changed to prediction intervals.

Q: What is quantile coherency?

A: It is the coherent loss defined in Eq (57) in appendix F.3, but computed w.r.t. one particular quantile estimation in different levels. For example, $loss = q_\{\alpha\}^\{v_1\}(x) - [q_\{\alpha\}^\{v_2\}(x) + q_\{\alpha\}^\{v_3\}(x)]$, where vertex 1 is the parent vertex and 2, 3 are child vertices.

Q: "Building this connection to the combined point forecast regularizes each quantile estimation to be more coherent". Why is that the case? Did you prove it theoretically or experimentally?

A: We have shown this empirically in section 4.3 and Figure 5 (c), since the quantile coherency can be improved as the point forecast coherency improved.

Q: Why are the weights between 0 and 1?

A: The weights are softmax outputs from gating networks.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the authors for their responses. Unfortunately, in its current form, I still believe the paper is not ready for publication. See additional comments below.

> We agree that some parts of section 3.2 should not appear in the main text as they are too detailed. We will update that section with more conceptual explanations. The rest of your concerns are addressed below:

The problem is not "the details" but the clarity of this section and the paper in general. 

> [Inconsistency of statements] 

Sorry, we misunderstood your statements. You were referring to two different papers: Ben Taieb & Koo, 2019, and Taieb et al, 2017.

> [Probabilistic forecast coherency and quantile coherency] "Probabilistic forecast coherency refers to the coherency of each quantile, which is defined the same as the coherency of the mean forecast.". 

Your definition of probabilistic coherency is still not clear. Your answer to Reviewer CTFm to the same question does not help either. Can you give a precise definition of "your" quantile and probabilistic coherency?

> "MECATS is valid under a weaker assumption, so it works better in practice".

What does "valid" mean? I think you are referring to "coherency". The same applies to MinT. Even if the forecasts are biased, MinT is still "valid" (coherent). However, MinT gives additional guarantees if the forecasts are unbiased. Since you do not give guarantees, you cannot compare with MinT on that point.

> "We intended to compare with ... but their state-of-the-art implementations are not available."

Given that a link to the code was provided to you, a comparison with the state-of-the-art methods (Rangapuram et al. (2021) and Taieb et al. (2017)) is important for future versions of the paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer tXgU
content.comment:
Thank you very much for your reply! We would love to improve our paper on the matter you have mentioned. Here we make some clarifications on the questions you have:

1. [Clarity of Section 3.2] We understand that we are not presenting this section in its best way, but here is a short intuition: our objective function of multi-quantile forecaster in Eq (4) contains an integral, so we wish to do a Chebyshev approximation (much like using Taylor expansions for polynomial functions, Chebyshev is commonly used as an approximation in numerical integration, more details can be found [here](http://inis.jinr.ru/sl/m_mathematics/mref_references/mason,%20hanscomb.%20chebyshev%20polynomials%20(2003)/c0355-ch08.pdf)). Eq (8) is the approximation result for each quantile forecaster. One only needs to estimate the coefficients $C_k$ of Chebyshev polynomials using neural networks.

2. [Quantile Coherency] The term "probabilistic coherency" hasn't appeared in our paper, we only have quantile coherency and what we meant by that is to compute coherency of forecasts at each corresponding quantile level, just like computing the coherency for the mean forecasts. As for "probabilistic forecast" we also mean multiple quantile forecasts: if this causes confusion, we will make these more aligned in the future.

3. [Comparison with MinT] We agree with your argument, MinT provides a hard constraint and guarantees the results to be coherent with or without unbiasedness. MECATS only has a soft constraint and achieves near coherent results. So MECATS can only be compared with SHARQ in this matter. But we want to highlight the fact that MinT does not perform well empirically (at least not as well as MECATS) in many situations. Besides the unbiasedness assumption, MinT forces the forecasts to be aligned without considering the inherent noise of each time series realization: they are all likely the reason for inferior performance in real applications.

Please let us know if you still have any questions/concerns. We thank you again for your suggestions on improving our papers.

Sincerely,

Authors

display_title: Official Review of Paper383 by Reviewer CTFm

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method that combines forecasts from different models and aims to produce coherent forecasts subject to hierarchical constraints imposed in advance.
content.main_review:
Overall the paper was well written and attempted to solve very practical problems. 
However, I am unsure about a few key basic assumption of the methods: (1) why the point forecast should be ideally subject to additive constraints? (2) misalignment between the evaluation losses and the training objective functions.
Thus I think the paper could be a stronger publication in future if those key design was addressed.

Some more details comments:
(1)	On page 1, ‘A well-generalized forecasting model should not only...’, it’d be good to either add references to elaborate why ‘accuracy’ is not sufficient – was it because generalization concerns or was it because application requirements?

(2)	On page 3, the condition following ‘Ideally, the forecasts should satisfy’is not well motivated – it suggests that for any given point forecasts x, we should consider the constraint that the point forecast should follow additive condition. However, this claim was not sound – the claim would be correct assuming all point forecasts are mean estimates by the linearity of expectation, but what if the point forecast is a quantile forecast? In the quantile cases, the equality doesn’t have to hold unless further assumptions.

(3)	In Section 3.1, should ‘confidence intervals’ be replaced with ‘prediction intervals’?

(4)	In Proposition 1, it makes a strong assumption of ground truth should follow in the intervals of min and max of point forecasts. Such assumption was impractical and not well motivated – for example, if the point forecasts are all mean forecasts, the probability of the realization falling into the intervals of X mean forecasts could never be 1 and thus the assumption would never guarantee to hold. With such unrealistic assumption, I could not see the value of the proposition. This issue was consistent with the findings in Section 4.3 ‘we found it not easy to eliminate the coherent loss...’.

(5)	In Section 4.1, it’d be good to add what objective functions were used for some of the point forecast models.

(6)	In Section 4.1, need to add reference for the four public datasets.

(7)	In Section 4.1, it’d be good to add why MASE was chosen to evaluate the forecasts – if MASE was used for evaluation, why can’t it be used as an objective function into the models? What about evaluating for quantiles other than median estimates?

content.title: Response to Reviewer CTFm
content.comment:
We thank you for your comments and helpful suggestions. Your concerns are addressed below:

(1) [Additive constraints] In our paper we meant “accuracy for a single time series is not sufficient” (please refer to lines 9-10 of section 1) instead of meaning accuracy as an evaluation metrics is not sufficient. It is clear in our context that forecasting hierarchical time series needs to consider information from adjacent aggregation levels or the hierarchy overall, rather than treating each time series separately. This is also the reason we incorporate multilevel information into our training objective. This problem has been discussed in many past literatures (e.g., [1]), and our work is also driven by an application from a large corporation.

(2) [Additive point forecasts] We were aware that quantile forecasts are not additive, as we have already mentioned in section 4.3. So, by point forecast, we explicitly refer to mean forecast, as we have used expectation for that in the paragraph after equation 1.

(3) Q: In Section 3.1, should ‘confidence intervals’ be replaced with ‘prediction intervals’?

A: Yes, thanks for spotting this :)

(4) [Proposition 1] We wish to clarify that $\hat{x}_{v_i}$ is a scalar instead of a vector, i.e., at a particular timestamp instead of a realization within a time range. So, we do NOT mean one vector strictly dominates the others. If you could refer to appendix A for more details, this assumption is equivalent to coherent error $\delta$ for each expert cannot be all strictly positive or negative. So we can cancel $\delta$ out to obtain coherent results.

(5) [Objective functions] The objective function of the gating network (Equation 2, where $L_{v_i}$ is $L$-2 loss) is our primary objective, as MECATS is model-free, there is no assumption on how each individual expert is trained. Indeed, we follow the standard procedure/default objective functions of the libraries to train each expert, it is possible that some experts might be down-weighted given the misalignment of the objective function with gating networks. But in most cases the forecasting API is encapsulated, one is not allowed to modify the internal objective. We could also do an ablation study on the influence of different gating network objective functions for each expert’s weight, but this is not the primary focus of our work. 

(6) [Reference for public datasets] Please see appendix F.2.

(7) [MASE as evaluation metric] MASE is commonly used as an evaluation metric for time series forecasting accuracy, it belongs to the family of relative error measures, which has advantages over some other measures as discussed [here](https://robjhyndman.com/papers/mase.pdf). The reasons MASE is not used as an objective function of gating networks are 1. It measures the accuracy of single time series, without considering hierarchical information; 2. MASE is $L$-1 loss, the gradient of this objective is constant. If this is used to train a relatively large neural network, the speed of convergence would be very slow. We were aware of this problem in the very beginning and proposed to use $L$-2 loss (Equation 2) to warm up and then use $L$-1 loss to fine-tune the model. There is no significant difference between the results obtained using this method and our current reported results. For CRPS and quantile losses, it has been shown that they are equivalent, you can find the proof [here](https://shorturl.at/dlpJK).

[1] Hyndman et al (2011), optimal combination forecasts for hierarchical time series.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a mixture of experts approach to hierarchical time series forecasting. The main contribution of the paper is to use a gated network to combine predictions from specific expert models. An additional contribution is the addition of quantiles using a model-free approach that avoids quantile crossing.
content.main_review:
The paper does present novel and coherent contributions. The empirical results present quite a detailed exposition of experiments in both paper and supplementary material.

- The paper is well written and structured
-Method is compatible with other state of the art forecasting methods such as FBProphet
 

The main weakness of the proposed model is that the overall probabilistic forecasts might still be subject to the dominance of weak experts at test time. Have the authors' considered sparsity control at test time perhaps on the basis of some measure of predictive quantile width? This is likely to be an issue in low data regimes. 
- authors also do not thoroughly investigate the quality of uncertainty estimates emanating from their method using NLLs etc.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a novel method in hierarchal time series forecasting. This is an understudied area in literature. The paper provides an empirical evaluation of the method. Two potential pitfalls of the work include the potential dominance of weak exports and the lack of evaluation of the quality of uncertainty estimates.

content.title: Response to Reviewer apbf
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments! Below are the answers to your concerns:

1. [Dominance of weak expert] Weak experts also get lower weights at test time, since the weights are obtained from the validation set that represents the generalization of each expert. So, there will not be any dominance issues.

2. [Test data] Apart from the change of dynamic experiment where the experts’ weights are updated in an online manner, we are assuming the test data follows the same distribution as training data. Situations such as data drift are not the primary focus of this paper. In addition, the combination of a diverse set of experts brings more robustness to the forecasts and is therefore helpful to data drift.

3. [Evaluation of uncertainty estimates] We have evaluated our uncertainty estimates in section 4.2 using CRPS, which can also be found in Figure 4 and table 1, and section H from the appendix. We wish to emphasize that CRPS is commonly used as a metric of probabilistic forecasts, as can be found in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.04743.pdf.
